planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed into well-drained, average soil in full sun; this shrub flowers on new growth within its first year and tolerates light trimming to control its sprawling habit.

directions: Plant container specimens in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun along a dry streambed-style slope or border; orange trumpet bush is an Andean relative of yellow esperanza (Tecoma stans) native to dry riverbeds from Peru to northwestern Argentina, producing slender, tubular, deep orange to orange-yellow flowers in loose terminal clusters through warm weather. It grows as a semi-evergreen to evergreen shrub reaching roughly 8-15 feet, blooming most heavily once nighttime temperatures stay warm. Established plants tolerate drought and brief cold dips into the mid-20s F, resprouting from the base after a hard freeze. Prune after flowering flushes to maintain a compact shape and encourage repeat bloom cycles.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, limestone-derived or alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; this Caribbean limestone-forest tree needs frost-free conditions to establish.

directions: Plant container specimens in well-drained, limestone-based or alkaline soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky coastal forests it inhabits in Cuba, Hispaniola, and the Bahamas. Cuban jacaranda is a smaller-statured relative of the common jacaranda, reaching about 15-40 feet, with similarly fern-like compound leaves and clusters of fused, pubescent, purple-blue trumpet flowers in spring. It is markedly more drought- and limestone-tolerant than Jacaranda mimosifolia, making it a good choice for coral-rock or alkaline coastal gardens in the warmest zones. Protect young trees from any frost, as this species has essentially no cold tolerance below the low 30s F.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct-sow seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun in spring; this seasonally dry-tropics species prefers a pronounced dry period to trigger its heaviest bloom.

directions: Direct-sow seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Brazilian jacaranda is native to the dry woodlands of Bolivia, Brazil, and northern Argentina and is distinguished from the common jacaranda by its more pointed leaflets and denser, fuller clusters of deep violet-blue flowers that open at the start of the rainy season. The broad, globose crown and moderately fast growth make it a popular park and street tree throughout its native range and in other seasonally dry subtropical regions. It responds well to a distinct dry season followed by rain, which concentrates and intensifies flowering compared to trees grown in consistently irrigated landscapes. Site it where its wide-spreading crown has room, away from pavement that could be lifted by surface roots.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant grafted or vegetatively propagated specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun in spring; seed-grown plants revert to the standard blue-purple flower color, so only cutting-grown or grafted stock reliably produces white blooms.

directions: Plant grafted or cutting-grown nursery specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun; 'Alba' is a rare sport of the common jacaranda that replaces the species' signature lavender-blue flower clouds with pure white to cream trumpet blooms, opening on bare branches in late spring before the fern-like foliage fully emerges. Growth habit, mature size, and cultural needs match the standard blue-flowered tree, but 'Alba' must be propagated vegetatively, since seedlings do not come true to the white flower color. The lightly fragrant flowers stand out dramatically against the tree's pale gray bark, making it a striking specimen tree distinct from the ubiquitous purple-flowering form. Give it the same frost protection as the species, since tops can be damaged below the mid-20s F.

planting.note: Plant grafted specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; seed-grown African tulip trees are color-variable, so only grafted stock reliably produces true golden-yellow flowers.

directions: Plant grafted nursery specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; 'Aurea' is a golden-yellow-flowered selection of the African tulip tree, bearing the same large, upright, cup-shaped flower clusters as the species but in warm gold tones streaked with orange rather than the typical scarlet-orange of wild seedlings. Because color is inconsistent from seed, this form is propagated by grafting onto seedling rootstock to guarantee true yellow blooms. Growth rate, mature size, and cultural requirements mirror the standard orange-flowered tree, including its fast growth and tendency to need space for a wide, spreading canopy. As with the species, check local invasive-species regulations before planting, since the orange form has naturalized aggressively in parts of the tropics.
